text: "I knew you to be a hard man… and I was afraid." A wrong view of God came first; the fear came after.
explanation:
In the parable of the talents, two servants said, "Lord, you delivered to me five talents… two talents," giving their master the credit, and they doubled what they'd been given. The third said, "I knew you to be a hard man" (the word means harsh, stern), "and I was afraid, and went and hid your talent." Nothing in the story says the master was harsh. It was the servant's picture of him.

How you see God affects everything: how you use your gifts, how you handle money, how you serve. Long before fear of the future, fear of sickness or fear of lack, there's usually a hard picture of God. See Him as He really is, and fear loses its root.

text: "You shall fear the Lord your God," says Deuteronomy. Jesus quoted it as "You shall worship the Lord your God."
explanation:
When the devil offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship, Jesus answered from Deuteronomy. But where it said "fear the Lord," He said "worship the Lord." He was showing us what the healthy fear of God really is: not the dread you feel toward a snake, but reverent worship.

Adam hid because he was afraid of God's voice. That isn't the fear God wants. "The fear of the Lord prolongs days": the more you worship Him, the longer and fuller your life. Draw near; don't hide.

text: Your need is your title to His grace. He has all the supply; you only have to admit you're in need.
explanation:
In the Old Testament, God provided, forgave and healed, but from behind the veil. In Jesus, God stepped out among people: forgiving sinners face to face, healing in the crowds, sitting at the table as the loaves multiplied. Whenever He met someone in real need, all of heaven's resources flowed toward them. The woman who touched His hem received all she needed.

Positive and negative attract. Pride says, "I'm fine, I'm not depressed, I don't need help," and receives nothing. In Nazareth they rejected Him, and He walked away, taking with Him the healing of the broken-hearted. Don't pretend. Bring Him your need.

text: The only time the Gospels say Jesus was angry, it wasn't at a sinner. It was at hard hearts with no grace for a man in need.
explanation:
A man with a withered hand was in the synagogue, and the Pharisees watched to see whether Jesus would heal him on the Sabbath, not whether He could. Even His enemies counted on Him to do good. Jesus "looked around at them with anger, being grieved by the hardness of their hearts," then said, "Stretch out your hand," and it was restored.

Not once does Scripture say He was angry at the woman caught in adultery or any repentant sinner. What angered and grieved Him was a lack of grace. And even in that anger, He healed. His anger is never His main nature; His mercy endures forever.

text: "The king's wrath is like the roaring of a lion." The devil "walks about like a roaring lion," impersonating an angry God.
explanation:
God has sworn He will never again be angry with those who are in Christ; His wrath was exhausted at the cross. So when you hear an accusing voice saying, "God is angry with you, that's why things are going wrong," recognise the roar. The devil goes about like a roaring lion, imitating the King's wrath, "seeking whom he may devour."

He can only devour those who believe him. That's why the verse just before says, "casting all your care upon Him, for He cares for you." The moment you forget that God cares for you, you become an easy target. Remember it, and the roar is just noise.

text: What grieves the Holy Spirit? Paul says it right there: words that don't impart grace.
explanation:
"Let no corrupt word proceed out of your mouth, but what is good for necessary edification, that it may impart grace to the hearers. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God." People often claim the Spirit is grieved by all sorts of things. But Scripture ties it to words that withhold grace. It's the same word used of Jesus being grieved at hard hearts.

If a lack of grace grieves Him, grace gladdens Him. Grace is undeserved favour: praising your spouse when they haven't earned it, encouraging your child before the good results. "If you greet only your brethren, what do you do more than others?" Speak grace.

text: Look on the cross and see what God thinks of your sin. Look on Jesus and see what God thinks of you.
explanation:
Isaiah 53 shows the Servant wounded for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities. Isaiah 54 follows: "As I have sworn that the waters of Noah would no longer cover the earth, so have I sworn that I would not be angry with you, nor rebuke you." God doesn't need to swear, but He did, to strengthen your faith.

"Having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved from wrath through Him." God still corrects His children, gently, as a loving Father. But He is no longer angry with you, and He never will be. Every time you see a rainbow, remember that oath.
